lessons.title: useState Semantics: Replace, Batch, Function
lessons.explanation:
> **Simulation convention (no real React here):** the grader has no React or DOM.
> A "component" is a **pure function** `(props) => element` and an element is a plain object
> `{ type: string, props: object, children: array }` — children holds strings or more elements.
> Hooks are modeled as **pure state-transition logic**: plain functions over plain data.


## What `setState` actually does

Three rules explain 90% of useState bugs:

1. **Replace, not merge.** `setUser({ name: 'Ada' })` makes the state exactly `{ name: 'Ada' }`. Unlike class-component `this.setState`, nothing is merged — any field you leave out is gone.
2. **Updates are scheduled, then batched.** Calling `setCount(count + 1)` twice in one handler reads the *same* stale `count` both times — you get +1, not +2. React re-renders once, after the handler.
3. **Functional updates see the latest value.** `setCount(prev => prev + 1)` receives whatever the pending state is, so two of them really do add 2.

### Worked example

```js
// count is 0 when the handler fires
function handleClick() {
  setCount(count + 1);          // schedules "set to 0 + 1"
  setCount(count + 1);          // schedules "set to 0 + 1" again — still reads 0!
  setCount(prev => prev + 1);   // schedules "whatever is pending (1) + 1"
}
// after the batch: count === 2
```

Line by line: the first two calls close over the render-time value `count = 0`, so both schedule "become 1". The third is a **function**, so React calls it with the pending value `1` and it returns `2`. One re-render happens at the end with `count === 2`.

We model this as pure logic: an **updater** is a function `prev => next`. You will write updaters and a tiny scheduler that applies a queue of updates the way React does.

### Common mistakes

- Writing `setCount(count + 1)` inside intervals/timeouts and wondering why it only moves once (stale closure).
- Spreading nothing: `setUser({ age: 31 })` silently deletes `name` — replace, not merge.
- Expecting state to change immediately after calling the setter; the new value arrives on the next render.

lessons.title: The Immutable Update Catalog
lessons.explanation:
## Why mutation breaks React

React decides "did state change?" by comparing **references** (`Object.is`). If you `push` into the array you already hold, the reference is identical — React sees "no change" and skips the re-render, or memoized children keep rendering stale props. The rule: **every update produces a new object/array along the changed path**; untouched branches are reused as-is.

### Worked example: update one todo in a list

```js
function toggleDone(todos, id) {
  return todos.map(t =>
    t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t
  );
}
```

Line by line: `map` always returns a **new array** (new outer reference). For the matching todo we build a **new object** with spread, flipping `done`. Every other todo is returned **unchanged** — same reference, so memoized rows for them can skip re-rendering. New references exactly along the changed path, old references everywhere else: that is the whole discipline.

### The catalog (learn these cold)

| intent | tool |
|---|---|
| add to array | `[...arr, item]` / `[item, ...arr]` |
| remove from array | `arr.filter(...)` |
| update item in array | `arr.map(...)` with spread |
| insert at index | `[...arr.slice(0, i), item, ...arr.slice(i)]` |
| update object field | `{ ...obj, field: value }` |
| update nested field | spread **each level**: `{ ...o, a: { ...o.a, b: v } }` |
| remove object key | `const { gone, ...rest } = obj` |

### Common mistakes

- `push`, `splice`, `sort`, `reverse` mutate. Use spread/`filter`/`map`/`toSorted`/`toReversed`.
- Spreading only the top level and mutating a nested object — spread is **shallow**.
- Copying when nothing changed. If the item is not the target, return it as-is.

lessons.title: Thinking in Reducers (useReducer)
Derived State: Compute, Don’t Store
lessons.explanation:
## The redundancy rule

If a value can be **computed** from props or existing state, do not store it in state. Store the minimal facts; derive everything else during render:

```js
// BAD: three states that can disagree
const [todos, setTodos] = useState([]);
const [doneCount, setDoneCount] = useState(0);     // redundant!
const [visible, setVisible] = useState([]);        // redundant!

// GOOD: one source of truth, two derivations
const [todos, setTodos] = useState([]);
const [filter, setFilter] = useState('all');
const doneCount = todos.filter(t => t.done).length;        // derived
const visible = filter === 'all' ? todos : todos.filter(t => t.done === (filter === 'done'));
```

Why the "bad" version is a bug factory: every code path that changes `todos` must ALSO remember to update `doneCount` and `visible`. Miss one and the UI contradicts itself. Derived values can never drift — they are recomputed from the source every render.

The functions that compute derived values are called **selectors**: pure functions `(state) => view`. They are trivially testable and shareable.

### When computing is expensive

Recompute-every-render is the default. When a derivation is genuinely heavy, memoize it: cache the last inputs and the last result, recompute only when an input changed. That is all `useMemo` is — you will build the mechanism (`memoizeLast`) yourself below.

### Common mistakes

- Mirroring a prop into state (`useState(props.user)`) — the copy goes stale when the prop changes.
- Storing a filtered/sorted copy of a list you also store.
- Reaching for `useMemo` on cheap derivations — the cache costs more than the recompute.

lessons.title: What Belongs in an Effect?
lessons.explanation:
## Three homes for your code

Every line in a component lives in one of three places, and most useEffect bugs are code in the wrong home:

1. **Render** (the component body): computing what to show. Pure. Derivations live here — never in an effect.
2. **Event handlers**: code that runs *because the user did something* — submit, click, type. Side effects caused by an interaction (POST the form, show a toast) belong HERE, not in an effect watching a flag.
3. **Effects** (`useEffect`): code that synchronizes the component with an **external system** — subscriptions, timers, manual DOM, analytics on mount, syncing to localStorage. "After render, make the outside world match my state."

```js
// smells: effect reacting to an interaction flag
const [submitted, setSubmitted] = useState(false);
useEffect(() => { if (submitted) postOrder(cart); }, [submitted]);  // BAD
// the POST belongs in the submit handler:
function handleSubmit() { postOrder(cart); }                         // GOOD
```

## Dependency arrays

The second argument controls **when the effect re-runs**, compared entry-by-entry with `Object.is`:

- **no array** — after *every* render.
- **`[]`** — after the first render only (no dep can ever change).
- **`[a, b]`** — after renders where `a` or `b` changed since the last run.

React re-runs the effect when **any** entry differs from the previous render's entry. You will implement that exact comparison (`depsEqual`) below — it is a shallow, positional, `Object.is` walk, which is why inline objects/arrays in deps re-fire every render.

### Common mistakes

- Deriving state in effects (`setFullName(first + last)`) — compute in render instead.
- Omitting a dep the effect reads (stale closure) or "fixing" the lint warning by deleting the array.
- Objects/functions recreated each render used as deps — the effect re-fires every time.

lessons.title: Cleanup Functions & Effect Order
lessons.explanation:
## Every setup needs a teardown

An effect that subscribes, starts a timer, or opens a connection must return a **cleanup function**. React calls it:

- **before the effect re-runs** (deps changed), and
- **on unmount**.

```js
useEffect(() => {
  const unsubscribe = bus.subscribe(roomId, onMessage);  // setup
  return () => unsubscribe();                            // cleanup
}, [roomId]);
```

The lifecycle for a `roomId` change from `'a'` to `'b'`:

```text
mount:        setup('a')
deps change:  cleanup('a')  →  setup('b')     ← old torn down BEFORE new is built
unmount:      cleanup('b')
```

Walk that trace: the cleanup that runs is always the one **returned by the previous setup** — it closed over the old `roomId`, so it unsubscribes the OLD room. Forget the cleanup and every room change ADDS a subscription: messages double, then triple. That is the leak StrictMode's double-mount is hunting.

We simulate all of this with a **fake event bus** that records calls, and with plain closures — no React needed to reason about ordering.

### Common mistakes

- Returning nothing from an effect that subscribes — the #1 leak.
- Returning the WRONG thing: `return bus.subscribe(...)` only works if subscribe returns the unsubscriber; `return unsubscribe()` (calling it!) tears down immediately.
- Assuming cleanup runs only at unmount — it runs before EVERY re-run.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.instructions: State is `{ name: 'Ada', age: 36 }`. The handler calls `setUser({ age: 37 })`. What is the state after the re-render?
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.explanation: useState REPLACES the state with exactly what you pass — there is no merging. To keep the other fields you must spread them yourself: `setUser(prev => ({ ...prev, age: 37 }))`. (Class `this.setState` merged; the hook does not.)
Both calls read the same render-time `count` (5) from the closure, so both schedule "become 6". To actually add twice, pass functions: `setCount(prev => prev + 1)` twice gives 7.
Functional updates form a chain: React feeds each updater the result of the previous one. 5 → 6 → 7. This is why "next state depends on current state" should ALWAYS use the `prev =>` form.

The interval callback closes over the FIRST render's `count` (0) forever — a stale closure. Every tick schedules "become 0 + 1". The fix is a functional update, `setCount(prev => prev + 1)`, which never reads the stale variable.

The setter schedules a re-render; it does not reassign the local variable. `count` in this closure is still the value from the render that created the handler: 0. The new value is only visible in the NEXT render.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.instructions: Export `appendMessage(msg)` that RETURNS AN UPDATER: a function taking the previous array of messages and returning a NEW array with `msg` added at the end. The previous array must not be mutated. Usage: `setMessages(appendMessage("hi"))`. Example: `appendMessage("hi")(["a"])` → `["a", "hi"]`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.explanation: This is an updater FACTORY — `setMessages(appendMessage(text))`. The factory captures `msg`; the returned updater copies `prev` with spread so the old array is untouched. React compares references to decide whether anything changed, so the new array is essential.
hints: Return a function: prev => [...prev, msg].
Spread prev into a new array literal, then add msg.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.instructions: Export `incrementUpTo(max)` that returns an updater `prev => next` adding 1 but never exceeding `max`. Example: `incrementUpTo(3)(2)` → `3`, `incrementUpTo(3)(3)` → `3`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.explanation: A closure-captured `max` parameterizes the updater. The pattern: configuration goes in the factory arguments, state flows through the returned function. Reducers and middleware use the same shape.
hints: Return prev => Math.min(max, prev + 1).

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.instructions: Export `mergeState(prev, patch)` that returns a NEW object with the patch's fields layered over the previous fields (what class setState did automatically). Neither input may be mutated. `mergeState({a:1,b:2},{b:3})` → `{a:1,b:3}`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.explanation: Spread order is the rule: later spreads win, so `{ ...prev, ...patch }` keeps old fields and overwrites patched ones. Because useState replaces, you write this merge explicitly — usually inline as `setUser(prev => ({ ...prev, ...patch }))`.
hints: Spread prev first, then patch, into a new object literal.
Later spreads win: { ...prev, ...patch }.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.instructions: Export `setField(prev, field, value)` that returns a NEW object identical to `prev` except that `field` (a string key) now holds `value`. `prev` must not be mutated. `setField({email:""}, "email", "a@b.c")` → `{email:"a@b.c"}`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.explanation: The computed-property syntax `[field]: value` lets one generic updater serve every input in a form. This single function replaces a dozen hand-written `setEmail`/`setPassword` handlers — the standard controlled-form pattern.
hints: Spread prev into a new object and use a computed key: [field]: value.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.instructions: What is the difference between `useState(buildBigList())` and `useState(() => buildBigList())`?
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.explanation: Arguments are evaluated before the call, so `useState(buildBigList())` recomputes the list every render and throws the result away after the first. Passing the function itself (a lazy initializer) lets React call it exactly once. (To store a function IN state you would need `useState(() => fn)`.)

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.instructions: Export `resolveUpdate(current, update)` that models how React interprets one setState argument: if `update` is a function, return `update(current)`; otherwise return `update` itself. (Tests only pass values here; the function case is covered in the challenge.) `resolveUpdate(5, 9)` → `9`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.explanation: This one ternary IS the useState contract: a function argument is treated as a transition from the current value; anything else replaces the value outright. (It is also why you cannot naively store a function in state — React would call it.)
hints: Check `typeof update === 'function'`.
Function → call it with current; anything else → return as-is.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.instructions: Export a function `cycleTheme` that cycles the theme: 'light' → 'dark' → 'system' → 'light' → … Any value outside the cycle returns 'light'.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.explanation: Cycling is a transition that MUST read the previous value, so it has to be a functional update: `setTheme(cycleTheme)`. Writing `setTheme(theme === "light" ? ... )` inline at three call sites is how the cycle order drifts apart.
hints: Three-way branch — or find prev's index in an array and take (i + 1) % 3.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.instructions: Export a function `markAllSeen` that takes the previous notifications state `{ unread, lastSeenId }` plus a `latestId`, and returns a new object with `unread: 0` and `lastSeenId: latestId`. `markAllSeen({unread:4,lastSeenId:7}, 11)` → `{unread:0,lastSeenId:11}`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.explanation: Even when you overwrite every current field, keep the spread: the day a third field joins this state object, this updater keeps working instead of silently deleting it — the replace-not-merge lesson, applied defensively.
hints: Spread prev, then overwrite the two fields.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.instructions: Export a function `addPoints` that takes the previous `{ level, points }` and earned points; returns a new object where points accumulate, and every full 100 points converts into +1 level with the remainder kept (e.g. `{level:1,points:80}` + 50 → `{level:2,points:30}`).
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.explanation: Two fields that must change TOGETHER (level and points) are one state object with one updater — splitting them into two useState calls would let a render see "leveled up but points not yet reset".
hints: total = points + earned; levels gained = Math.floor(total / 100); leftover = total % 100.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.instructions: Export a function `pushRecent` that takes the previous array of recent searches and a new term: returns a new array with the term at the FRONT, any existing copy of it removed, and at most 3 entries total. `pushRecent(["a","b","c"], "d")` → `["d","a","b"]`; `pushRecent(["a","b"], "b")` → `["b","a"]`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.explanation: Three catalog moves fused: dedupe (filter), prepend (spread), cap (slice) — all non-mutating, so the whole policy is one readable expression. Every "recent items" dropdown you have ever seen runs this updater.
hints: filter the term out, spread it to the front, slice(0, 3).

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.instructions: Export a function `toggleSelection` that models clicking a row that selects it, or deselects when it was already selected: takes the previously selected id (or null) and the clicked id, returns the clicked id — or null when they match. `toggleSelection(null, 3)` → `3`; `toggleSelection(3, 3)` → `null`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.explanation: Selection state is just "the selected id or null" — not a parallel array of booleans. A single comparison implements select, switch, and deselect at once, and the state cannot contain two selected rows by construction.
hints: One ternary comparing the two ids.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.instructions: Export `applyUpdaters(initial, updaters)` where `updaters` is an array of functions `prev => next`. Apply them left to right, starting from `initial`, and return the final value. `applyUpdaters(0, [x => x + 1, x => x * 10])` → `10`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.explanation: Each updater receives the output of the one before it — exactly how React drains its update queue. `reduce` expresses "thread a value through a list of transformations" in one line, and the empty-array case falls out for free (reduce returns the seed).
hints: This is a fold: reduce over the updaters.
reduce((state, u) => u(state), initial).

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.instructions:
Export `simulateBatch(initial, updates)` that models how React commits one batch:
- `updates` is an array whose entries are either plain VALUES or updater FUNCTIONS.
- Walk the array in order, keeping a pending state that starts at `initial`:
  a function entry becomes `pending = fn(pending)`; any other entry becomes `pending = entry`.
- Return `{ state, renders }` where `state` is the final value and `renders` is `1`
  when at least one update changed the pending state at some point, else `0`
  (React skips the re-render when nothing ever changed — compare with `Object.is` after each step).

Examples: `simulateBatch(0, [1, p => p + 1])` → `{ state: 2, renders: 1 }`;
`simulateBatch(5, [5, p => p])` → `{ state: 5, renders: 0 }`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/us.explanation: You just rebuilt the useState commit loop: resolve each update against the pending value (functions see the chain, values replace it), and render only if some step produced a different value under `Object.is`. The "changed then changed back" test is the subtle part — React bails out only when NOTHING ever differed, which is why the flag latches rather than comparing first-to-last.
hints: Loop over updates keeping `pending`; resolve each entry like resolveUpdate did.
Track a boolean `changed`; set it whenever Object.is(next, pending) is false BEFORE assigning.
A batch that changed and changed back still renders — the flag latches on, it never resets.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: A handler runs `todos.push(newTodo); setTodos(todos);`. Why does the list on screen not update?
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: After `push`, `todos` is the SAME array object React already has in state. `Object.is(old, new)` is true, so React skips the update entirely. `setTodos([...todos, newTodo])` creates a new reference and fixes it.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Which of these array methods does NOT mutate the array it is called on?
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: `filter` (like `map`, `slice`, `concat`, `toSorted`, `toReversed`) returns a new array. `sort`, `splice`, and `reverse` rearrange the array in place — never call them directly on React state; copy first or use the `to*` variants.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: Spread copied the top level, so reassigning `copy.name` leaves `user.name` as 'Ada'. But `address` was copied BY REFERENCE — both objects point at the same nested object, so mutating `copy.address.city` also changes `user.address.city` to 'Paris', and the identity check prints true. This is why nested updates must spread every level.
hints: Spread copies one level deep. Which parts are shared?

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Export `addItem(list, item)` returning a NEW array with `item` appended at the end. The input array must not be mutated. `addItem([1,2], 3)` → `[1,2,3]`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: `[...list, item]` builds a brand-new array: a new outer reference (so React re-renders) whose elements are the SAME references as before plus the new one. Copying the container without cloning the contents is exactly right — and cheap.
hints: Spread the old list into a new array literal and add the item.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Export `prependItem(list, item)` returning a NEW array with `item` at the FRONT (newest-first feeds). Do not mutate the input. `prependItem([2,3], 1)` → `[1,2,3]`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: Position inside the new literal controls position in the result. `unshift` would do this in place — the immutable spelling is `[item, ...list]`, used constantly for activity feeds and notification stacks.
hints: Same spread trick, item first: [item, ...list].

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Export `removeById(list, id)` where `list` is an array of objects with an `id` field. Return a NEW array without the matching item (unchanged list contents otherwise, same order). Do not mutate. If no item matches, return a new array with the same items.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: `filter` returns a new array of the SURVIVORS, so the predicate is `item.id !== id` (note the NOT — a classic off-by-logic bug is filtering `===` and deleting everything else). The kept items are the same object references, which is ideal.
hints: filter keeps what the predicate says yes to — keep everything whose id is NOT the target.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Export `updateById(list, id, patch)` returning a NEW array where the object whose `id` matches gets the fields of `patch` merged over it (new object), and every other element is passed through unchanged. Do not mutate anything. `updateById([{id:1,qty:1}], 1, {qty:2})` → `[{id:1,qty:2}]`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: The map-with-ternary shape is the single most common immutable update in React code. New array, new object for the one changed row, identical references for the rest — memoized row components skip re-rendering untouched rows.
hints: map over the list; for the match return { ...item, ...patch }, otherwise return item as-is.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Export `toggleDone(todos, id)` where each todo is `{ id, text, done }`. Return a NEW array where the matching todo has `done` flipped (new object); others pass through unchanged. No mutation.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: The patch here derives from the item itself (`!t.done`), which is why the spread copy must happen FIRST conceptually: read the old value, write the new object. Mutating `t.done = !t.done` would pass the value tests but corrupt the original — the mutation check catches it.
hints: Same shape as updateById, but the patch is computed from the old item: done: !t.done.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Export `setCity(user, city)` where `user` looks like `{ name, address: { city, zip } }`. Return a NEW user object whose `address` is ALSO a new object with `city` replaced and `zip` kept. Do not mutate `user` or `user.address`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: Spread is shallow, so every level along the changed path needs its own spread: new user object, new address object, new city value. `name` is carried by the outer spread and the inner object reuses `zip`. Deeper nesting than two levels is a hint to flatten your state or use a reducer.
hints: Spread twice: once for user, once for user.address.
{ ...user, address: { ...user.address, city } }.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Export `removeKey(obj, key)` returning a NEW object with every field of `obj` except `key`. Do not mutate `obj`. `removeKey({a:1,b:2}, 'a')` → `{b:2}`. Removing a missing key returns a new equal object.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: Computed destructuring `{ [key]: _removed, ...rest }` peels one dynamic key off and gathers everything else into a fresh object. The alternative — `const copy = { ...obj }; delete copy[key];` — is also immutable-safe because `delete` runs on the copy, never the original.
hints: Destructure the doomed key out and rest-collect the survivors.
const { [key]: _x, ...rest } = obj; return rest;  (or copy with spread and use delete on the COPY).

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Export `insertAt(list, index, item)` returning a NEW array with `item` inserted so it ends up AT position `index`, shifting later elements right. No mutation. `insertAt(["a","c"], 1, "b")` → `["a","b","c"]`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: `slice` never mutates, so cutting the array at the index and reassembling `before + item + after` is the immutable `splice`. Index 0 and index `length` fall out naturally because `slice(0, 0)` and `slice(length)` are both empty.
hints: slice the list into before/after at the index and rebuild around the item.
[...list.slice(0, i), item, ...list.slice(i)].

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Export `replaceAt(list, index, item)` returning a NEW array where position `index` holds `item` and everything else is unchanged. No mutation. `replaceAt([1,2,3], 1, 9)` → `[1,9,3]`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: Mapping on the INDEX instead of a field is the positional twin of updateById. Modern JS also ships `list.with(index, item)` which does exactly this; either passes. The trap being avoided: `list[index] = item` mutates state in place.
hints: map's callback gets the index as the second argument.
Or: list.with(index, item) — the built-in immutable replace.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Export `moveItem(list, from, to)` returning a NEW array where the element at index `from` has been removed and re-inserted so it ends up at index `to` (indexes refer to positions in the ORIGINAL list for `from`, and in the list-after-removal for `to` — the standard drag-and-drop convention). No mutation. `moveItem(["a","b","c"], 0, 2)` → `["b","c","a"]`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: The copy-then-mutate-the-copy idiom: `splice` is fine as long as its target is a fresh array you own. Two splices (remove, insert) read far clearer than nested slice arithmetic, and the original state array is never touched — which the tests verify.
hints: Copy first, then you may use mutating methods ON THE COPY.
splice(from, 1) removes and returns the element; splice(to, 0, el) inserts it.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Export `toggleTag(tags, tag)` for an array of unique strings: return a NEW array with `tag` removed if present, or appended at the end if absent. No mutation. `toggleTag(["a","b"], "b")` → `["a"]`; `toggleTag(["a"], "b")` → `["a","b"]`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: Checkbox groups, multi-select filters, and favorite buttons are all this one function. Both branches return a new array — even the "remove" branch — so React always sees a fresh reference when the selection changed.
hints: Check membership with includes, then branch: filter it out, or spread it in.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Export `incrementQty(cart, id)` where `cart` is an array of `{ id, qty }`. Return a NEW array where the matching line has `qty + 1` (new object) and other lines pass through. If no line matches, append `{ id, qty: 1 }`. No mutation.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: Upsert = update-or-insert, and each arm uses the catalog entry you already know: map-with-spread for update, spread-append for insert. Deciding WHICH arm first (via `some`) keeps each branch simple instead of one clever unreadable expression.
hints: Two cases: the line exists (map + spread) or it does not (spread + append).
some() answers "is it already in the cart?".

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Export `sortedByPrice(products)` where each product is `{ name, price }`. Return a NEW array sorted by ascending price. The INPUT ORDER must be preserved in the original array (no mutation — plain `sort` mutates!). Equal prices keep their relative order.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: `sort` rearranges in place, which silently reorders your state array — a notorious React bug because everything LOOKS fine until an unrelated re-render. Copy-then-sort (or `toSorted`) gives you the sorted view while the state keeps its canonical order.
hints: Copy first ([...products]) then sort the copy — or use toSorted.
Numeric comparator: (a, b) => a.price - b.price.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Export `addUnique(list, item)` returning a new array with `item` appended — unless an identical primitive is already present, in which case return a new array with the same contents. No mutation. `addUnique(["a"], "a")` → `["a"]`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: Half of toggleTag: only the "absent" branch adds. Note both branches return a fresh array here because the exercise demands it; in production you might return `list` unchanged when the item exists so React can skip the render — both are defensible contracts, just be consistent.
hints: includes() to check, then either copy or copy-with-append.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Export `markAllDone(todos)` returning a new array where EVERY todo `{ id, text, done }` has `done: true` (each a new object). No mutation.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: When every row changes, every row gets a new object — map plus spread with no ternary. Remember the arrow pitfall: `(t) => { ...t, done: true }` is a syntax error (block body); wrap the object in parentheses.
hints: map with no condition — every element gets the spread treatment.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Export `clearDone(todos)` returning a new array containing only the todos with `done: false`, in order. No mutation.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: A bulk remove is still just filter — the predicate describes who STAYS. The kept todos ride through as the same references, so memoized rows do not re-render when their neighbors disappear.
hints: filter keeps the survivors: !t.done.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Export `applyDiscount(products, category, pct)` where products are `{ name, category, price }`: return a new array where every product IN that category gets `price` multiplied by `(1 - pct)` (new object; e.g. pct 0.1 = 10% off), others pass through unchanged. No mutation.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: Same shape as updateById with a broader predicate — the condition can be anything. The untouched branch returning `p` as-is matters even more here: in a 10,000-product list a category update should produce exactly as many new objects as there are matches.
hints: map-with-ternary, but the condition matches a GROUP rather than one id.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Export `renameProject(workspace, projectId, name)` where workspace is `{ name, projects: [{ id, name }] }`. Return a new workspace whose `projects` is a new array with the matching project renamed (new object). Workspace name and non-matching projects unchanged. No mutation.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: Array-inside-object is the most common nesting in app state, and the update composes mechanically: new workspace (spread), new projects array (map), new project object (spread). Three new references, one per level of the changed path.
hints: Object spread outside, map-with-spread inside — two catalog entries composed.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Export `appendCapped(log, entry, max)` returning a new array with `entry` appended, keeping only the LAST `max` entries. No mutation. `appendCapped([1,2,3], 4, 3)` → `[2,3,4]`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: Negative slice counts from the end, so `slice(-max)` is "the last max entries" regardless of length — and it never throws on short arrays. Chat windows, toast queues, and undo stacks all cap state exactly like this so memory cannot grow unbounded.
hints: Append first, then slice(-max) keeps the tail.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Export `newestFirst(events)` returning a new array with the events in reverse order. The input must keep its order (plain `reverse()` mutates!).
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: `reverse` is in the mutator family with `sort` and `splice`. Copy-then-reverse (or `toReversed()`) preserves the canonical append-order in state while the UI shows newest-first — storing the reversed array instead would force every insert to think backwards.
hints: Copy with spread, then reverse the copy — or use toReversed().

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: Export `mergeById(local, server)` — both arrays of `{ id, ... }`. Return a new array with every local item REPLACED by the server item of the same id when one exists (the server object itself is fine), otherwise kept; then any server items whose id is not in `local` appended in server order. No mutation of either input. Order: local order first, then new server items.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: Reconciling a server response with local state is a daily task in data-heavy UIs (and the heart of what react-query does). The map keeps local ORDER stable — users hate rows jumping — while content refreshes, and genuinely new rows land at the end. All with non-mutating tools.
hints: Two passes: map local (replace when the server has the id), then append server items with unseen ids.
A Set of local ids makes the "is it new?" check O(1).

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions:
This module exports three cart helpers, and ALL THREE mutate their input. Fix them so each
returns a new array/object without touching the input, with identical results:
- `addLine(cart, line)` — currently uses push
- `clearCart(cart)` — currently uses length = 0
- `setNote(order, note)` — currently assigns a property
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: Three mutations, three catalog entries: append → spread-append, clear → return a NEW empty array (the old one may still be rendered somewhere), set field → object spread. Notice `clearCart` needs no input data at all; returning `[]` is both correct and the cheapest possible update.
hints: Each fix is one line from the catalog.
Empty state is just a fresh empty literal — [] — not a gutted old array.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions: In `toggleDone` built with `map` + spread, non-matching todos are returned as the SAME object references. Why is that a feature, not laziness?
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: Reference stability is information: a row component wrapped in `React.memo` compares its `todo` prop by reference, so unchanged rows bail out instantly. Deep-cloning everything would be "safe" but would destroy that signal and force the whole list to re-render.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.instructions:
A kanban board is stored as:
`{ columns: { [colId]: { id, title, cardIds: [...] } }, cards: { [cardId]: { id, text } } }`

Export `moveCard(board, cardId, fromCol, toCol)` returning a NEW board where `cardId` is
removed from `columns[fromCol].cardIds` and APPENDED to `columns[toCol].cardIds`.
Requirements:
- `board`, `board.columns`, both affected column objects, and both cardIds arrays must all be fresh along the changed path; `board.cards` and unaffected columns must be the SAME references.
- No input mutation anywhere.
- If `fromCol === toCol`, return the board unchanged (same reference is fine).
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/im.explanation: This is the full discipline on a realistic normalized store: fresh objects on the changed path (board → columns → two columns → two arrays), untouched references everywhere else (cards, other columns). The reference-identity test is exactly what React.memo and useSyncExternalStore-based selectors rely on in production apps.
hints: Spread the board, spread columns, rebuild exactly two column entries.
Source column: filter the id out. Target column: spread-append the id.
Do NOT touch board.cards — reuse the reference by just spreading the board.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.instructions: What is the correct signature and contract of a reducer?
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.explanation: A reducer takes the current state and one action and RETURNS the next state. Pure means: no mutation of inputs, no side effects (no fetch, no timers, no random), same inputs → same output. That purity is what makes reducers trivially unit-testable.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.instructions: A reducer receives an action whose `type` it does not recognize. What should it do?
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.explanation: Return the same `state` reference: React sees no change and skips the re-render. Returning `undefined` would DESTROY the state, and a needless fresh copy forces a pointless re-render. (Throwing is a style some teams use in dev, but the convention — and what these exercises require — is pass-through.)

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.explanation: ADD 5 → 15. UNDO hits the default arm, so state stays 15 (printed again). RESET → 0. ADD 2 → 2. Dispatching is just repeatedly folding actions through the reducer — which is why the whole history of a UI can be replayed from its action log.
hints: UNDO is not a case the reducer knows — what does default do?

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.instructions: Export a function `addItem` that is an ACTION CREATOR: `addItem('sku1', 2)` returns the plain action object `{ type: 'ADD_ITEM', id: 'sku1', qty: 2 }`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.explanation: Action creators centralize the action's shape: every dispatch site calls `dispatch(addItem(id, qty))` and can never misspell `'ADD_ITEM'` or forget a field. They are plain functions returning plain objects — nothing magical.
hints: Return an object literal with a fixed type string plus the two payload fields.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.instructions: Export a function `removeItem` that is an action creator: `removeItem('sku1')` returns `{ type: 'REMOVE_ITEM', id: 'sku1' }`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.explanation: Shorthand property syntax (`{ type: ..., id }`) keeps creators one-liners. When the reducer and the creators agree on shapes, the action vocabulary becomes a typed protocol between UI and state.
hints: One fixed type string, one payload field.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.instructions: Export a function `setQty` that is an action creator: `setQty('sku1', 5)` returns `{ type: 'SET_QTY', id: 'sku1', qty: 5 }`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.explanation: Note what is NOT in the action: the new cart. Actions carry the minimal facts of the event (which line, what quantity); computing the resulting state is the reducer’s job. Keeping that split is what makes action logs replayable.
hints: Same pattern: fixed type, two payload fields.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.instructions:
The cart state is an array of lines `{ id, qty }`. Export `cartReducer(state, action)` handling ONE action for now:
- `{ type: 'ADD_ITEM', id, qty }`: if a line with that id exists, return a new array where that line's qty is increased by `action.qty` (new object); otherwise append `{ id, qty }`.
- Any other action type: return `state` unchanged.
No mutation.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.explanation: A reducer case is just an immutable update selected by `action.type` and parameterized by the action payload. The braces around the case body let you declare `const exists` without leaking across cases — a habit worth keeping in every switch-reducer.
hints: This is the upsert from last lesson, driven by action fields.
some() to detect the existing line, then map+spread or spread-append.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.instructions:
Export `cartReducer(state, action)` (state: array of `{ id, qty }`) handling the FULL union:
- `{ type: 'ADD_ITEM', id, qty }` — upsert as before (existing line: qty + action.qty; else append).
- `{ type: 'REMOVE_ITEM', id }` — drop the line.
- `{ type: 'SET_QTY', id, qty }` — set the line's qty to exactly `action.qty`; if qty is 0 or less, REMOVE the line instead.
- `{ type: 'CLEAR' }` — empty cart.
- anything else — return `state` unchanged.
No mutation anywhere.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.explanation: The whole cart domain now lives in one pure function: every rule (upsert, remove, the "qty 0 means remove" policy) is here and nowhere else. Handlers shrink to `dispatch(setQty(id, n))`, and the policy is testable with plain asserts — no component rendering required.
hints: One case per action type; each body is a one- or two-line catalog move.
SET_QTY with qty <= 0 is business logic INSIDE the reducer: reuse the REMOVE logic (filter).

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.instructions:
A checkout wizard's state is `{ step, data }` where `step` is 0..2 and `data` is an object of collected fields.
Export `wizardReducer(state, action)`:
- `{ type: 'NEXT' }` — step + 1, clamped to 2.
- `{ type: 'BACK' }` — step - 1, clamped to 0.
- `{ type: 'SET_FIELD', field, value }` — merge `{ [field]: value }` into `data` (new object), step unchanged.
- `{ type: 'RESET' }` — return `{ step: 0, data: {} }`.
- unknown — return `state`.
No mutation.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.explanation: Two shapes of state (a number and a nested object) in one reducer: clamping lives in NEXT/BACK, the nested double-spread in SET_FIELD, and RESET just returns the canonical initial state literal. Wizards are the textbook useReducer case — many related transitions over one small object.
hints: NEXT/BACK are clamped arithmetic on step; spread the rest of state.
SET_FIELD needs two spreads: state AND data (nested update).

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.instructions: useReducer's third argument is an `init` function: `useReducer(reducer, savedIds, init)` computes the initial state from an argument ONCE. Export `init(savedIds)` that takes an array of ids and returns the cart state `[{ id, qty: 1 }, ...]` — one line per saved id, each with qty 1. `init(['a','b'])` → `[{id:'a',qty:1},{id:'b',qty:1}]`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.explanation: The init function converts raw persisted data (ids from localStorage, a server snapshot) into real state shape, and React calls it exactly once. The parentheses around the object literal matter: without them the arrow body `{ id, qty: 1 }` parses as a block, not an object.
hints: map each id to an object. Wrap the object literal in parentheses: (id) => ({ id, qty: 1 }).

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.instructions:
A reducer case does:
```js
case 'TOGGLE':
  state.open = !state.open;
  return state;
```
The state really does change in memory. What does the user see?
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.explanation: React compares the returned reference with the previous one; they are identical, so it skips the re-render. The in-memory object silently changed, so the NEXT unrelated update suddenly shows the flipped value — the "UI is one step behind" bug. (Option 4 describes a symptom you may see later, but the direct answer is: no update happens.)

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.instructions:
This todo reducer has two classic bugs:
1. `ADD` mutates the state array with push.
2. Unknown actions return `undefined` (falls off the end of the switch).
Fix both. Behavior: `{ type: 'ADD', todo }` appends the todo immutably; `{ type: 'REMOVE', id }` filters by id; anything else returns the state unchanged.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.explanation: Both bugs are silent at first: the mutation bug "works" until React bails out of a render, and the missing default only bites when an unexpected action arrives and wipes state to `undefined`. The strictEqual test pins the exact contract: unknown action → the very same reference back.
hints: push → spread-append.
Add a default arm that returns state.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.instructions: Export `runActions(reducer, initial, actions)` that folds an array of actions through a reducer, returning the final state. `runActions(r, 0, [a1, a2])` is `r(r(0, a1), a2)`. Also return the initial state untouched for an empty log.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.explanation: The name "reducer" comes from this: `(state, action) => state` is literally a `reduce` callback. Folding a log of actions from an initial state reconstructs the current state — the idea behind time-travel debugging, event sourcing, and Redux devtools replay.
hints: A reducer has EXACTLY the signature Array.prototype.reduce wants.
actions.reduce(reducer, initial) — one line.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.explanation: Reducer state does not have to be an object: a number works, and returning a number IS the new state. The floor rule in DECREMENT shows business invariants living in transitions — no caller can produce a negative count.
hints: State can be a bare number — the reducer pattern does not require objects.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.explanation: "Name-or-null" guarantees at most one modal is ever open — a boolean per modal could open three at once. Choosing a state SHAPE that makes bad states impossible does more than any amount of careful handler code.
hints: State is "the open modal’s name or null". TOGGLE compares before deciding.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.explanation: Tabs show why reducers beat scattered setters: OPEN, SELECT, and CLOSE all maintain the invariant "active is always an open tab (or empty)". With separate setOpen/setActive calls in handlers, one missed branch leaves active pointing at a closed tab — the ghost-tab bug every editor has shipped at least once.
hints: CLOSE_TAB has two concerns: the list (filter) and possibly the active pointer (last survivor or empty string).

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.instructions: Which action design is best for "the user submitted the quantity form with value 5"?
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.explanation: Actions carry the minimal FACTS of the event; the reducer owns deriving the next state. A whole-next-state action moves the logic back into every dispatch site (and makes the log useless for replay); reading the DOM in a reducer destroys purity; raw values lose the type tag that routing depends on.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.explanation: false, true, Grace. The handled action produced a NEW object (s1 !== s0 → React re-renders); the unknown action returned the very same reference (s2 === s1 → React bails out). Reference identity is the signaling channel between your reducer and React.
hints: A handled action builds a new object; an unhandled one returns the input itself.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.instructions: Which situation is the STRONGEST signal to move from useState to useReducer?
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.explanation: useReducer shines when MANY transitions share one piece of state: the logic concentrates in a testable pure function and components just dispatch events. A lone boolean is fine as useState; expensive init is solved by lazy initializers; multiple independent states are often better left separate.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.instructions:
Export `withUndo(reducer, initial)` that wraps ANY reducer in undo support. It returns a NEW reducer
over the wrapped state shape `{ past: [], present: initial }`:
- `{ type: 'UNDO' }`: if `past` is non-empty, pop the last entry — it becomes `present`, and `past` loses it. If `past` is empty, return the state unchanged (same reference).
- any other action: delegate to the inner reducer. If the inner reducer returns a DIFFERENT value than `present` (compare with `Object.is`), push the old present onto `past` and store the result as `present`. If it returns the same value, return the wrapped state unchanged (same reference).
No mutation of `past` arrays — copy on every change.
The returned reducer must also expose nothing else; initial wrapped state is built by the caller as `{ past: [], present: initial }`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/re.explanation: A higher-order reducer wraps any domain logic with a cross-cutting feature — undo here, logging or persistence elsewhere — without the inner reducer knowing. The two strict no-op tests encode the efficiency contract: when nothing changed, return the SAME state so React can bail out, and never record non-changes in history (otherwise UNDO appears to "do nothing" to users).
hints: This is a HIGHER-ORDER reducer: a function returning a reducer that calls the inner one.
UNDO: new past = past.slice(0, -1); new present = last element of old past.
Delegate: const next = reducer(state.present, action). Only record history when Object.is(next, present) is false.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions: A component stores `items` in state AND stores `itemCount` in state, updating both in every handler. What is the idiomatic fix?
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: `items.length` is a derivation — just compute it in render; it can never be out of sync. The useEffect version "works" but renders twice (once stale, once synced) and adds a whole effect for what one expression does. This effect-to-sync-state pattern is the #1 useEffect anti-pattern.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions: A child does `const [user, setUser] = useState(props.user)` so it can display the user. The parent later passes a different `props.user`. What does the child show?
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: useState reads its initializer ONLY on mount; later prop changes never touch that state. The child is frozen on the first user — the classic prop-mirroring bug. If you only display it, use `props.user` directly; copy into state only when the child intentionally forks the value (e.g. an editable draft).

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: Each "render" recomputes the counts from the single source of truth, so they are correct by construction: 0/1, then 1/1, then 2/0. There is no second copy that could have been forgotten — the whole argument for deriving.
hints: Just run the selector against each successive state.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions: Export a selector `selectDoneCount` that takes an array of todos `{ text, done }` and returns how many are done.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: A selector is nothing but a pure read over state. filter+length reads naturally; `todos.reduce((n, t) => n + (t.done ? 1 : 0), 0)` avoids the intermediate array if you care.
hints: filter by done, take length (or reduce a counter).

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions: Export a selector `selectCartTotal` that takes cart lines `{ id, priceCents, qty }` and returns the order total in cents.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: Storing the total in state alongside the lines is the classic drift bug (change a qty, forget the total). As a selector the total is always right, and the same function serves the cart badge, the checkout page, and the tests.
hints: reduce: sum += priceCents * qty.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions: Export a selector `selectFullName` that takes a user `{ firstName, lastName }` and returns `'firstName lastName'`, trimmed so a missing/empty part leaves no stray space. `{firstName:'Ada',lastName:''}` → `'Ada'`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: Formatting belongs in derivations, not in state. `trim()` quietly handles the empty-part edge cases that an interpolation would render as " Hopper" — a tiny selector earning its unit test.
hints: Concatenate with a space, then trim.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions: Export a selector `selectOverdue` that takes an array of tasks `{ title, dueDay }` and a number `today`, and returns the TITLES of tasks whose `dueDay` is strictly before `today`, in input order.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: filter→map chains ARE the selector language. Note the strict `<`: a task due today is not overdue. Parameterized selectors (state + an argument like `today`) are still pure — same inputs, same output.
hints: filter, then map to the title.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions: Export a selector `selectByStatus` that takes an array of tickets `{ id, status }` and returns an object counting tickets per status, e.g. `[{id:1,status:'open'},{id:2,status:'open'}]` → `{ open: 2 }`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: Dashboards are selectors all the way down: the tickets array is the state; every widget (counts, percentages, worst-offender lists) derives from it on render. `?? 0` seeds each first occurrence.
hints: Loop and count into an object: counts[status] = (counts[status] ?? 0) + 1.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions: Export a selector `selectMaxPrice` that takes products `{ name, price }` and returns the highest price, or 0 for an empty array.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: Price-slider bounds are a derivation of the catalog, not state. Seeding reduce with 0 makes the empty case safe; `Math.max(...[])` alone would give -Infinity.
hints: reduce with Math.max, seeded with 0 — or Math.max(0, ...products.map(p => p.price)).

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions: Export a selector `selectIds` that takes an array of objects with `id` fields and returns just the array of ids, in order.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: Projections this small still earn a name: `selectIds(items)` reads better than an inline map at six call sites, and when the id field is renamed there is one place to change.
hints: One map.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions: Export a selector `selectCompletionPct` that takes todos `{ done }` and returns the completed percentage as a whole number (Math.round), with 0 for an empty list. `[{done:true},{done:false}]` → `50`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: Progress bars are pure derivations. The empty-list guard matters because `0 / 0` is NaN — and a NaN silently poisons every calculation downstream instead of throwing.
hints: Guard empty first (0/0 is NaN), then round done/total * 100.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions: Export a selector `selectUnreadCount` that takes messages `{ id, readAt }` (readAt is a timestamp number or null) and returns how many have `readAt === null`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: The badge number in every inbox UI. Storing `unreadCount` next to `messages` is double bookkeeping; deriving it means marking a message read is ONE state change, not two that can be forgotten separately.
hints: filter on readAt === null, take length.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions: Export a selector `selectTotalsByCategory` that takes expenses `{ category, amount }` and returns an object mapping each category to the summed amount. `[{category:'food',amount:10},{category:'food',amount:5}]` → `{ food: 15 }`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: Group-and-aggregate is the chart-feeding selector: the pie chart, the per-category list, and the "top category" headline all derive from this one function over the raw expense rows.
hints: Accumulate into an object: totals[cat] = (totals[cat] ?? 0) + amount.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions: Export a selector `selectCanSubmit` that takes a form-errors object (field → error string or null) and returns true only when EVERY value is null. `{email: null, pw: null}` → `true`; `{email: "bad", pw: null}` → `false`. An empty object → `true`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: The submit button’s disabled state is derived from the errors object — never a separate `canSubmit` boolean kept in sync by hand. `every` on an empty array is true, which gives the right answer for a form with no validated fields yet.
hints: Object.values + every.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions: Export a selector `selectBreadcrumb` that takes a path string like '/shop/books/scifi' and returns the segment array ['shop', 'books', 'scifi'] (empty segments removed; '/' → []).
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: The breadcrumb trail derives from the route — UI state you never store. split-then-filter handles leading, trailing, and doubled slashes in one pass, all edge cases the naive split leaves as empty crumbs.
hints: split('/') produces empty strings around slashes — filter them out.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions: Export a selector `selectCheapestInStock` that takes products `{ name, price, stock }` and returns the NAME of the cheapest product with `stock > 0`, or null when nothing is in stock. First wins on price ties.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: Filter-then-min in one loop. The strict `<` is what makes ties stable (first stays best), and returning null — not undefined, not throwing — gives the UI an explicit "sold out" case to render.
hints: One pass: track the best candidate; strict < keeps the first on ties.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions: Export a selector `selectBusiestDay` that takes an object mapping day names to visit counts and returns the day with the most visits (first key wins ties; assume at least one entry). `{mon: 5, tue: 9}` → `'tue'`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: Headline stats ("busiest day: Tuesday") are object-shaped derivations. Object.entries turns the map into iterable pairs; the tie rule falls out of using strict > rather than >=.
hints: Object.entries + a running best; strict > keeps the first on ties.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions: Export a selector `auditState` that is a design-review helper: given an object describing a component's stored state fields as `{ field: 'source' | 'derived' }`, return the array of field names marked 'derived' — the ones that should NOT be stored. `{todos: 'source', doneCount: 'derived'}` → `['doneCount']`.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: A toy, but the audit it encodes is real: walk your useState calls and ask of each, "could I compute this from the others?" Every yes is a field to delete. Destructuring in the callbacks (`[, kind]`, `[name]`) picks the tuple halves cleanly.
hints: Object.entries, filter on the value, map to the key.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions: Export `visibleTodos(todos, filter)` where `filter` is `'all'`, `'active'`, or `'done'`. Return the todos to display: all of them, only `done: false`, or only `done: true` respectively. Input order preserved.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: State stores `todos` + the tiny string `filter`; the visible list is derived fresh each render. Storing the filtered copy instead would mean re-filtering on every toggle AND every todo edit — in two places. Note 'all' returns the same reference: a valid derivation does not need to copy.
hints: Branch on the three filter values; 'all' returns the input as-is.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions: Export `productView(products, minPrice)` where products are `{ name, price }`: keep only products with `price >= minPrice`, sorted by ascending price, WITHOUT mutating the input array. Ties keep input order.
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: Order of operations doubles as the mutation-safety argument: `filter` produces a brand-new array, so chaining `.sort()` onto it mutates only the derived copy, never the state. (Filtering fewer items before sorting is also cheaper.) If you sort FIRST you must copy first: `[...products].sort(...)`.
hints: filter first — it already returns a fresh array you own.
Then sorting that fresh array is safe: you never touch the input.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions: What does `useMemo(() => heavyCalc(data), [data])` actually do?
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: useMemo is a per-component cache of ONE previous result keyed by the dependency array. Same deps (compared with Object.is) → return the cached value; changed deps → call the function again. It affects neither threading nor whether the component re-renders.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions:
Export `memoizeLast(fn)` that wraps a single-argument function with a last-call cache:
- The first call invokes `fn` and remembers the argument and result.
- A call with the SAME argument (`Object.is`) returns the cached result WITHOUT calling `fn`.
- A call with a different argument invokes `fn` again and replaces the cache (cache size: 1 — calling with A, then B, then A calls `fn` three times).
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: This IS useMemo: one slot, Object.is comparison, recompute on change. The object-argument test demonstrates the deep consequence — a parent that recreates `{x: 1}` every render defeats the cache even though the data "looks" equal. That is why immutable updates that PRESERVE references for unchanged branches matter so much.
hints: Closure variables: lastArg, lastResult, and a has-run flag.
Compare with Object.is — reference equality for objects, exactly like React deps.
Why the flag? The very first call must compute even if the argument is undefined.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions: Inside a component: `const view = useMemo(() => filter(items, opts), [items, opts]);` where `opts = { min: 5 }` is created fresh in the same component body each render. How often does `filter` run?
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: Deps compare by Object.is. A new `{ min: 5 }` object every render is never the same reference, so the memo misses every time. Fixes: hoist the constant out of the component, memoize `opts` itself, or depend on the primitive `opts.min`.

bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.instructions:
One state object drives a product search page:
`{ products: [{ id, name, price }], query: '', sortDir: 'asc' | 'desc', page: 1, perPage: 2 }`

Export `searchView(state)` returning the fully derived view:
`{ items, total, pageCount, page }` where:
- matching = products whose `name` contains `query` case-insensitively (empty query matches all)
- `total` = number of matching products
- sorted by price according to `sortDir` (no input mutation; ties keep order)
- `pageCount` = ceil(total / perPage), minimum 1
- `page` = state.page clamped into [1, pageCount]
- `items` = the slice of sorted matches for that (clamped) page
bootforge/react-state/state-mechanics/de.explanation: Five UI facts (list, total, page count, current page, ordering) all fall out of ONE stored state via a pipeline of derivations — including the subtle rule that changing the query can force the current page back into range, which "stored page + stored results" designs always get wrong. The mutation test enforces the copy-before-sort discipline inside a derivation.
hints: Pipeline: filter → copy+sort → count → clamp page → slice.
pageCount must be at least 1 even with zero matches, or clamping breaks.
slice window: start = (page - 1) * perPage, end = start + perPage.

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.instructions: Where should "send the POST request when the user clicks Buy" live?
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.explanation: The POST is caused by an interaction, so it belongs in the handler. Routing it through state + effect adds an extra render, makes the intent invisible, and risks double-firing (e.g. when the flag is never reset). Effects are for synchronizing with external systems, not for reacting to your own events.

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.instructions: A component needs `fullName` whenever `firstName` or `lastName` change. Which implementation is right?
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.explanation: This is a derivation, not a synchronization — no external system is involved. The effect version stores redundant state and renders twice (stale, then corrected). One expression in render is always in sync and free.

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.instructions: Where does "subscribe to the chat server for room `roomId`, and resubscribe when it changes" belong?
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.explanation: A live connection is an external system that must track state — the definition of an effect. `[roomId]` makes React tear down the old subscription (via cleanup) and set up the new one whenever the room changes, and ALSO handles mount/unmount for free. A handler would miss roomId changes that do not come from that dropdown.

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.instructions: Where does "keep `document.title` equal to the unread count" belong?
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.explanation: The browser tab title is outside React — synchronizing it is effect work. Doing it in render is a side effect during a pure phase (breaks under StrictMode/concurrent rendering); doing it in every handler scatters one responsibility across the codebase. One effect, one dep.

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.instructions: What does `useEffect(() => { log(count); })` — NO second argument — do?
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.explanation: No array means "no condition": the effect runs after EVERY render. It is rarely what you want but it is valid JS. Note the difference from `[]`, which runs the effect once — the empty array and the missing array are opposites, a classic interview trap.

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.instructions: With `useEffect(() => { fetchProfile(userId).then(setProfile); }, [])` and a `userId` prop that later changes, what happens?
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.explanation: `[]` promises React "I depend on nothing" — so the effect runs once, closing over the first `userId` forever. When the prop changes, nothing re-fires: stale data bug. The honest deps are `[userId]`; the lint rule (`exhaustive-deps`) exists precisely to catch this lie.

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.instructions: Every render creates `const options = { retries: 3 };` and the component has `useEffect(connect, [options])`. How often does the effect run?
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.explanation: Deps are compared positionally with Object.is — reference equality for objects. A fresh literal every render never equals the previous one, so the effect re-fires every time. Fixes: depend on the primitive (`[options.retries]`), hoist the constant outside the component, or memoize it.

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.explanation: Primitives compare by value (true, true). Two object literals are two different references (false). The deliberate difference from ===: `Object.is(NaN, NaN)` is true while `NaN === NaN` is false — which is why React uses Object.is for deps and state bailouts: a NaN state value would otherwise "change" every render.
hints: Object.is is reference equality for objects, but it treats NaN specially.

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.instructions:
Export `depsEqual(prev, next)` — React's shallow dependency comparison:
- returns `true` when both arrays have the same length AND every position is equal.
- positions compare like `Object.is` (for the JSON-safe values in the tests, strict equality semantics are enough — but remember real deps use Object.is).
- different lengths → `false`.
(The reference-equality behavior for objects is tested separately in the next exercise.)
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.explanation: This is the entire algorithm React uses to decide whether your effect re-runs: positional, shallow, Object.is. Nothing recursive — which is exactly why a nested object that was recreated "looks changed" even when its contents are identical.
hints: Length check first.
every((v, i) => Object.is(v, next[i])).

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.instructions: Export `depsEqual(prev, next)` with the same contract as before (same length, positionally `Object.is`-equal). This version is tested with object references and NaN — make sure you use `Object.is`, not `===`.
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.explanation: The function-reference case is the daily-life version: a handler defined inline in the component body is a NEW function each render, so an effect depending on it re-fires every render. That is the problem useCallback exists to solve — it stabilizes the reference so depsEqual (this function!) returns true.
hints: Same code as before works — IF you used Object.is.
The NaN test fails with ===; Object.is handles it.

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.instructions:
Export `shouldRunEffect(prevDeps, nextDeps)` modeling React's complete decision for one effect:
- `nextDeps === null` (no array passed) → `true` (run after every render).
- `prevDeps === null` (first render — nothing to compare) → `true`.
- otherwise → `true` only when some position differs (same-length arrays assumed; compare with Object.is).
Examples: `shouldRunEffect(null, [1])` → `true`; `shouldRunEffect([1], [1])` → `false`; `shouldRunEffect([1], [2])` → `true`; `shouldRunEffect([], [])` → `false`.
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.explanation: Now all three dependency modes are one function: no array → always run; first render → always run; otherwise re-run only on a real change. `[]` falls out of the general rule — every() over an empty array is true, so it never re-runs after mount. No special case needed.
hints: Two null guards first — both mean "must run".
Then: run when NOT all positions are equal.

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.instructions: Export `changedDeps(prev, next)` that returns the array of INDEXES where `prev[i]` and `next[i]` differ (Object.is semantics; same length assumed). `changedDeps([1,"a",true],[1,"b",false])` → `[1,2]`. Great for answering "why did my effect run?".
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.explanation: This is a real debugging tool people write as a custom hook (`useWhyDidYouUpdate`): log which dependency index actually changed between renders. Nine times out of ten the culprit index points at an inline object or arrow function.
hints: Walk the indexes, collect the ones where Object.is fails.

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.instructions: Where does "persist the settings object to localStorage whenever it changes" belong?
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.explanation: localStorage is an external system, and "whenever it changes" is a synchronization condition — textbook effect with `[settings]`. Scattering the save across handlers means the one handler someone adds next year will forget it; the effect catches EVERY path that changes the state.

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.instructions: "Log a `page_view` analytics event once when the screen first appears." Which implementation?
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.explanation: Once-per-mount work is `[]`. In the render body it would fire on EVERY render (and during renders React may throw away); with no array, same problem. Note StrictMode will double-fire this in dev — idempotent analytics (or a dev-only dedupe) is the proper response, not removing the array.

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.instructions: "Track the window width in state so the layout can respond." What is the right structure?
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.explanation: Render reads of `window.innerWidth` miss resizes (nothing triggers a re-render), and option 3 is circular. The listener-in-effect is the pattern: subscribe once on mount, push changes into state, unsubscribe on unmount. (Polling works but burns CPU for worse latency.)

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.instructions: One effect currently both (a) subscribes to the chat room from `[roomId]` and (b) sends an analytics event from `[theme]` — so theme changes re-subscribe the chat. What is the fix?
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.explanation: Effects are grouped by SYNCHRONIZATION CONCERN, not by lifecycle moment. Two unrelated systems → two effects, each with its own minimal deps; now a theme change no longer tears down a chat connection. Omitting the dep (option 3) makes the analytics read a stale theme.

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.instructions:
Export `codeHome(description)` — a rules function for the three homes. Given one of these exact strings, return `'render'`, `'handler'`, or `'effect'`:
- 'compute the filtered list' → render
- 'format the title string' → render
- 'POST the form on submit click' → handler
- 'show a toast after delete succeeds' → handler
- 'subscribe to websocket messages' → effect
- 'sync the document title' → effect
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.explanation: The classification itself is the knowledge: derivations → render; interaction-caused side effects → the handler that knows the moment; external-system synchronization → effects. Writing it as a lookup table makes you commit each case to a category explicitly.
hints: A lookup object keyed by the exact strings is fine — the point is the categories.

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.instructions:
Export `depsFor(reads)` modeling the exhaustive-deps rule: given the array of reactive value names an effect's code reads, return the dependency array — the same names, sorted alphabetically, duplicates removed. Reading nothing returns `[]`.
`depsFor(['roomId', 'userId', 'roomId'])` → `['roomId', 'userId']`.
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.explanation: The lint rule is exactly this mechanical: the deps array IS the set of reactive values the effect reads — no additions, no omissions, no judgment calls. When the honest array re-runs too often, the fix is restructuring the code (split effects, move values out), never editing the array to lie.
hints: Set for dedupe, spread back to an array, sort.

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.instructions: "After a successful save, show a toast." The save happens in `handleSave` (an async handler). Where does the toast go?
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.explanation: The toast is a direct consequence of the interaction, and the handler already knows the exact moment of success — `await save()` resolving. The state+effect detour adds indirection and a double-fire risk. (Rendering a BANNER from `saved` state would be fine — that is UI, not an imperative side effect.)

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.instructions: In development StrictMode, React mounts, unmounts, and remounts each component, so your `[]` effect runs twice. What is this designed to catch?
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.explanation: The remount simulates "this component can be set up and torn down at any time". Code that survives it — because every setup has a matching cleanup — is correct; code that double-subscribes reveals a real production bug (the same thing happens on fast route toggles). Fix the cleanup, never suppress the double-run.

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.instructions:
Model a component's effect list across renders. Export `runEffects(prevState, effects)`:
- `prevState` is `null` on the first render, else the array returned by the previous call (one entry per effect: its last-run deps).
- `effects` is an array of `{ deps }` where `deps` is an array or `null` (no dep array).
- Return `{ ran, nextState }`: `ran` = array of effect INDEXES that run this render, `nextState` = array of each effect's deps for next time (store the deps as given, including null).
- Rule per effect (same as shouldRunEffect): run when its deps are null, when there is no previous state, or when any position changed vs the stored deps (Object.is).
Example: first render, two effects `[{deps: []}, {deps: [1]}]` → ran `[0, 1]`. Next render with `[{deps: []}, {deps: [2]}]` → ran `[1]`.
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/e.explanation: You built the bookkeeping React keeps for every component: a stored deps array per effect, refreshed each render, with a three-clause rule deciding what fires. Seeing `[]`, `[x]`, and "no array" fall out of ONE comparison function is the moment dependency arrays stop being folklore and become mechanics.
hints: Per effect: compute prevDeps (null when prevState is null), apply the shouldRunEffect rule.
nextState just stores this render’s deps verbatim — even null.
Collect indexes with forEach + push.

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/c.instructions: When does an effect’s cleanup function run?
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/c.explanation: Cleanup is the first half of every re-synchronization: tear down the old world, then set up the new one. Unmount is just the final teardown with no setup after it. "Cleanup = unmount only" is the misconception that causes doubled subscriptions when deps change.

bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/c.instructions: An effect with `[roomId]` deps runs for room "a", then `roomId` becomes "b". The cleanup that runs before the new setup — which `roomId` does it see?
bootforge/react-state/effects-and-data/c.explanation: The cleanup function is the return value of the PREVIOUS setup call, so its closure holds the previous render’s values. That is exactly what you want: it must unsubscribe the OLD room. This pairing — each setup owns its matching teardown — is why closures, not lifecycle methods, are the right tool.

`return unsub()` invokes the unsubscriber during setup and returns its result (undefined) as the "cleanup". The component is subscribed for roughly zero milliseconds. Correct: `return unsub;` — hand React the FUNCTION, do not call it.
